name: LGBTQ people and Islam
scope: LGBTQ people and Islam: what Islam is held to say about same-sex acts and gender-variant people, and the positions of Muslims on LGBTQ people, as Rahman (s1), Jaspal (s2) and Davies (s3) frame it. Two strands: (1) the mainstream traditional position, in which homosexuality is forbidden and stigmatized (Jaspal; Zafeeruddin, s5, a Hanafi mufti's account from Qur'an, hadith and law); (2) LGBT Muslim and queer reinterpretation, which rereads the sources, e.g. Kugle's Homosexuality in Islam (s4, s1), and denies that LGBT and Islam are incompatible (Davies). Where the two strands disagree a statement is a split or null. Excluded: Western politics of LGBT rights generally (homonationalism, Islamophobia) except as these sources tie it to Muslim positions, and non-Muslim views of Islam. Wikipedia only guided the search.

sources.title: Contemporary Same-Sex Muslim Sexualities: Identities and Issues (Handbook of Contemporary Islam and Muslim Lives, Springer; abstract page with reference list)
sources.author: Momin Rahman
sources.usedFor: Scholarly overview of same-sex Muslim sexualities: premodern homoeroticism, contemporary Muslim homophobia, LGBT Muslims in majority and minority cultures, theological reinterpretation; its reference list names the field's main works.

sources.title: Islam and Homosexuality (Wiley Blackwell Encyclopedia of Gender and Sexuality Studies, 2016; abstract, University of Brighton repository page, Wayback copy at web.archive.org/web/20260711020021/)
sources.author: Rusi Jaspal
sources.usedFor: Encyclopedia entry: homosexuality is highly stigmatized and in most cases forbidden in mainstream Islam; treats theological, social and psychological levels.

sources.title: Islam, Sexuality, and Gender Identity (encyclopedia entry; abstract on the Monash University repository page)
sources.author: Sharyn Graham Davies
sources.usedFor: Encyclopedia entry on LGBT and Islam: the common view that they are incompatible, and evidence against it.

sources.title: Homosexuality in Islam: Islamic Reflection on Gay, Lesbian, and Transgender Muslims (Pluralism Project bibliography entry for Kugle, Oneworld 2010)
sources.author: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University
sources.usedFor: Bibliographic record naming Kugle's book as a reading on gay, lesbian and transgender Muslims.

sources.title: Islam on Homosexuality (Darul Ishaat, Karachi, 1999; archive.org copy)
sources.author: Mufti Muhammad Zafeeruddin (translated by Syed Azhar Ali Zaidi)
sources.usedFor: A traditionalist Hanafi mufti's account of what Islam holds on homosexuality, from the Qur'an, hadith, history and medicine.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Zafeeruddin's chapter 'Punishment of Homosexuals in Islam' (pp. 85-88) gives the consensus verdict that both participants are to be put to death, with disagreement only over the manner, and says an Islamic government is duty bound to punish. He writes as a traditionalist mufti, and the queer-reinterpretation strand's sources (s1, s3, s4) are only abstracts that state no position on criminal law.

summary: Sources on LGBTQ people and Islam describe a mainstream traditional position, in which same-sex acts are forbidden in Islamic law and stigmatized, and a smaller strand of LGBT Muslim and queer reinterpretation that rereads scripture and rejects the claim that LGBT identity and Islam are incompatible. Traditionalist texts such as Zafeeruddin's prescribe punishment of homosexual acts up to death, left to the ruler's discretion in the manner, and confine sex to marriage between a man and a woman.

notes: Searched the five defining sources and Zafeeruddin's book (chapters on Islamic law, punishment of homosexuals, gazing, coverable limbs, marriage) and al-Qawim's 'Why Homosexuality is Prohibited in Islam' (2015) for every statement's topic. Only three statements are settled; the rest are null. Rahman, Jaspal, Davies and the Pluralism Project page are abstracts or catalogue records without text on specific positions, so the reinterpretation strand states no position on any statement. al-Qawim's book is not cited: its text never names the subject by its name or an alias and no two defining sources name it, so it fails the coatrack check, and it is mostly an anti-gay-rights polemic built on secular arguments. Not found: the Iranica entry 'Homosexuality ii. In Islamic law' and the full Encyclopaedia of Islam entry 'Liwat' (abstract only).
